summary:
Moquegua department stands under the national framework of Peru: the country does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. No Moquegua-specific trans law, ordinance, court finding or enforcement action appears in the sources, and the national rules bind the department.

Two legislative stages govern restroom access. On 20 February 2025 the Congress' Commission on Women and Family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar entry to public sanitary facilities designated for the sex other than one's birth sex, with exceptions only for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage; as of publication the measure still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho called the text discriminatory and warned that security staff would effectively judge people by personal criteria, such as demanding their DNI.

On 2 April 2025 the Congress plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, the dictamen of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes', whose article 5 bars from public sanitary facilities anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. An analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the IDEHPUCP institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru argues the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. The same analysis records that Congress has already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally and applies to the risk environment in Moquegua. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report counts 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected and hate crimes rising. It recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the bodies showed gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate.
tangentialFactors:
Hate-crime law offers LGBT people no coverage in Peru. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking such coverage.

A single case has produced a conviction. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu and found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
localsOnly:
The recorded violence figures understate incidence. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender and co-author of the 2024 report, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry, so residents face a risk environment worse than the published counts.

Facility access is decided at the door. Because article 5 conditions entry on biological sex and the February dictamen would require unambiguous signage, establishments in Moquegua must police restroom use, and Gianna Camacho's warning indicates that staff will rely on personal criteria such as asking for a DNI rather than any documented verification.

The health-guidance change of June 2024 removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, which bears on how trans residents are treated in healthcare settings in the department.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory describes any Moquegua-specific law, ordinance, court decision, police practice or establishment-level enforcement; whether restroom restrictions are actively enforced in the department, and by whom, is unresolved and not sourced.

The sources do not address legal gender marker or DNI amendment procedures for trans people in Moquegua or Peru; entry-screening practice beyond the reported risk of staff demanding a DNI is unresolved.

Whether the February 2025 dictamen on bills 6506 and 8457 subsequently received plenary backing is not stated in the inventory; the April 2025 law's article 5 is the sourced operative text.

The name Gianna Camacho appears in the inventory both as the trans-rights activist quoted against the February 2025 dictamen and as co-author of the 2024 report on rising hate crimes; whether these are the same person is unresolved.
